name: Nicholas II of Russia
summary: Nicholas II held that the tsar's authority was God-given and absolute, and he refused to share power with elected bodies in his 1895 speech and afterwards. Under pressure from the 1905 revolution he accepted the October Manifesto and a Duma, but he kept his powers and dissolved Dumas that opposed him. He promoted the Hague disarmament conferences, backed Russian expansion in the Far East, and led Russia into the First World War before abdicating in March 1917.

property-fundamental.rationale: January 1906: explicitly called all property rights inviolable.

strong-leader.rationale: He dissolved Dumas that opposed him in 1906 and 1907 and insisted that the autocracy be kept intact.

empower-police-military.rationale: His government used troops against the 1905 petition march and the revolution that followed; he kept the armed forces under his command.

decide-locally.rationale: In 1895 he rejected any role for elected zemstvo assemblies in government.

more-religion-public.rationale: June 15, 1915: proposed Orthodox processions throughout Russia.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: He promoted the Hague conferences that set up international arbitration machinery.

revolution-justified.rationale: Condemned the revolutionaries publicly in March 1905 and treated revolution as a threat to be suppressed.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In his 1895 speech to zemstvo delegates he vowed to keep absolute autocracy as his father had, treating hereditary monarchy as the basis of his rule.

democracy-best.rationale: December 1905: personally rejected universal suffrage as dangerously republican.

political-violence-never.rationale: Contested: he condemned revolutionary violence, but his government ordered troops to fire on demonstrators in 1905. The evidence points both ways.

separate-church-state.rationale: The 1906 laws kept his sweeping powers over church affairs, and the Orthodox Church stayed under imperial authority.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He supported expansion in the Far East, which led to the Russo-Japanese War.

national-self-determination.rationale: His government restricted Finnish autonomy through the 1899 February Manifesto despite a protest petition.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Dismissed responsibility when ministers sought proceedings against police pogrom organizer Podgorichani.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Rejected the idea that zemstvo assemblies should take part in government in 1895, and kept his authority as God-given rather than dependent on consent.

separated-powers.rationale: Under the 1906 system ministers answered only to him, and he dissolved the first two Dumas rather than share power.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: November 5: condemned police inaction against strike agitation.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Chose and dismissed ministers, and took personal command of the army in 1915.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Insisted that the monarch's position rested on hereditary succession and autocratic authority rather than on election.

collective-defense.rationale: He strengthened the Franco-Russian alliance, and in 1914 Russia went to war to support Serbia and its allies.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Held that as emperor by God's grace he had a sacred duty to uphold the autocracy and the Orthodox faith.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Kept sweeping executive powers as supreme autocrat after 1906, with ministers responsible only to him.

land-redistribution.rationale: Rejected taking landlords’ land; affirmed their inalienable ownership.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Inferred: he defended hereditary autocracy and dynastic succession.

elective-rulers.rationale: Kept the throne hereditary and rejected constitutional limits on the autocracy; he did not endorse choosing rulers by election.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Inferred: he opposed revolutionary resistance to the monarchy and kept his authority over the Duma.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Kept autocratic powers under the 1906 laws, including a veto and the right to dissolve the Duma, and treated parliament as subordinate to the monarch.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Reportedly warned the German ambassador about a worldwide Jewish–Masonic conspiracy.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He dissolved Dumas that opposed him and approved the 1907 electoral change that favoured conservative members.

participatory-democracy.rationale: In 1895 he rejected giving zemstvo delegates a voice in government and kept the Duma advisory until 1905.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Believed that God had chosen him as tsar and that his decisions reflected God's will, as biographers describe his outlook.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Passed the throne to his brother by the abdication manifesto, which upheld the dynasty's hereditary succession.

arms-reduction.rationale: His 1898 rescript proposed an international conference aimed at putting an end to the progressive development of armaments.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Opposed revolutionary change of the state and defended the existing monarchy.

national-church-status.rationale: Maintained the Orthodox Church's privileged status and pressed the Church to canonise Seraphim of Sarov in 1903.

notes:
Primary full texts (his diaries and letters to Alexandra and his mother, the 1895 speech in full) could not be read: the archive.org text was not accessible from this session, so the Nicholas quotes come from the Wikipedia article. Confidence is capped accordingly. The October Manifesto was drafted by Witte and issued under pressure; it is not counted as Nicholas's own position on the civil liberties it lists. Measures he personally drove (the 1906 and 1907 Duma dissolutions, the 1915 command) count; Stolypin's land reform is treated as Stolypin's measure, not Nicholas's. Antisemitism: secondary accounts say he privately welcomed the Kishinev mobs as a tool for unity, but that is a late, secondhand report, so no answer rests on it.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 7 answers taken from it, 14 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass. Existing answers were not read; only metadata, notes, sources and the blank-statement list were consulted. Downloaded and searched all 29 available monthly files of his 1914–1917 letters; editorial notes and Alexandra’s opinions are not treated as his statements. The October Manifesto and ministers’ economic reforms do not by themselves establish his own preferences. Searched the ten priority economic statements; only property-fundamental has direct evidence. Scarcity or food-price complaints do not establish rent control, public ownership, a job guarantee, capital controls, free trade or positive liberty. Economic freedom and the social function of property also remain unknown. Modern technology and ecology statements lack a documented matching position. Pardons establish personal responsibility for leniency, not that he ordered pogroms. No claim that he organized the pogrom wave is made. Property quotations are reported contemporary speeches, not high-confidence original transcripts. All remaining nulls reviewed against the full statement list.
